screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Basic Input
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how programs remember values, how to describe those values to the compiler, and how to get data from a person typing at the console. We'll treat a variable as a labeled box in memory: a name identifies the box, and the data type describes what kind of item fits inside. You'll see the core types every C programmer uses: whole numbers, single and double precision decimals, and single characters. Then we'll practice reading values with the standard input function and explain why the address-of operator is essential when storing user input. We'll also cover simple arithmetic, how integer division truncates results, and how casting lets you get precise floating-point answers. Together these skills let you build interactive programs such as calculators or small data collectors. By the end you will be able to declare and initialize variables, read and store user input correctly, and choose the right type and conversions to avoid common mistakes like segmentation faults or silent precision loss. Ready to build a memory model and work with real input? Let's explore the key topics that follow.

screens.title: Learning Objectives

I will show why initialization prevents unpredictable behavior and how to pick descriptive names. Second, you will distinguish the core C data types — whole numbers, single and double precision decimals, and character storage — and learn typical uses for each. Third, you will use the standard input function to read values typed by a user and understand why the address-of operator is required for scanf to place values into memory. Fourth, you will perform arithmetic and learn how integer division differs from floating-point division, plus how explicit casting fixes precision issues. Each objective includes a short practice or checkpoint so you can verify your competency. These skills are the foundation for building interactive command-line tools and safe numeric calculations, so mastering them now saves time and frustrating bugs later.

screens.title: What is a Variable in C?
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is a label for a location in the computer's memory where a value can be stored and changed while the program runs. Think of it like a labeled box on a shelf: the label is the variable name and the box holds a value of a particular kind. Declaring a variable tells the compiler the label and the kind of box you want. Initializing a variable means you put a starting value inside the labeled box right away, which avoids unpredictable contents. For example, declaring an integer named count reserves space for a whole number and initializing it to zero gives it a known starting state. A common beginner mistake is using a variable before it has been initialized, which leaves whatever data was already in that memory cell and can lead to confusing outputs or logic errors. When naming variables, choose descriptive names and follow the convention used in this course; in C, snake_case is common and names cannot start with digits or include special characters beyond the underscore. By mastering declaration and initialization you create reliable programs that behave predictably when they read, compute, and print values.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A variable is a named memory location; declaration reserves space and initialization assigns a safe starting value.

content.html:
Core Concept

Variables as labeled boxes

Declaration tells the compiler the label and type. Initialization places a known value inside the box so you avoid garbage data.

Declaration example
int score;  // declares an integer variable named score
Initialization example
int age = 30;  // declares and initializes age to 30
Key Takeaway

Always initialize variables before use to avoid unpredictable program behavior.

Analogy & Quick Rules
  • • Variable name: the label on the box. Use descriptive names like student_count.
  • • Data type: the box size and allowed contents (int, float, double, char).
  • • Declaration: reserve space. Initialization: place a known item inside.
  • • Naming rules: no leading digits, only underscore as special character, follow snake_case for readability.
Common mistake
Using a variable before it is initialized results in garbage values and unpredictable behavior. Initialize variables when declaring them when possible.
Check your understanding
Declare three variables for a student record: an integer id, a float GPA, and a char grade. Initialize them and print their values.

screens.title: Fundamental Data Types: int, float, double, char
screens.narratorSegment: C provides a small set of fundamental types that cover most beginner needs. The integer type stores whole numbers and is efficient for counts and indexes. Float is single-precision floating-point suitable for simple decimal values and when memory efficiency matters. Double is double-precision floating-point; it offers higher accuracy and is the default choice when precision matters. Character stores a single symbol and is often used for letters, digits, or to hold small integer codes. Each type uses a certain number of bytes which affects the range and precision. For example, integer division between two integers truncates any fractional part, so 10 divided by 3 becomes three. A common misuse is picking float when double is needed for accurate results, or assuming char stores multi-character strings. Another pitfall is forgetting the float literal suffix for some languages — in C, you often write 9.99f for a float literal, while doubles can be written without a suffix. Practice deciding a type for a scenario: counts use int, measurement with moderate precision can use float, scientific data should prefer double, and single typed symbols use char. This matching avoids precision loss and storage surprises.

keyIdea.title: Type guidance
keyIdea.text: Use int for whole counts, float for lightweight decimals, double for higher precision, and char for single characters.

content.html:
Definition

Core data types

int
Stores whole numbers. Use for counts and indexes. Example: int score = 5;
float
Single-precision decimal. Use when memory or precision constraints allow. Example: float temp = 23.5f;
double
Double-precision decimal. Prefer when you need accuracy. Example: double pi = 3.141592653589793;
char
Single character stored as a small integer code. Example: char initial = 'A';
Comparison & Examples
When to choose int: counts like number of students, loop indices, or status codes.
When to choose float: simple measurements where 6–7 digits precision is sufficient.
When to choose double: scientific or financial calculations needing greater accuracy.
When to choose char: single letter inputs, small markers, or components of a string.
Common misconception
Assuming char stores a string. A char holds one character; strings require character arrays or pointers. Also don't assume float precision equals double—results differ for division and accumulation.
Key Takeaway

Choose types to balance memory and precision; prefer double when accuracy matters.

screens.title: Using scanf() to Read User Input
screens.narratorSegment: Reading user input in C is commonly done with the standard input function that uses format specifiers to know what type to expect. The crucial detail is that scanf needs the memory address where the value should be stored. The address-of operator returns that memory address. For example, when reading an integer you place the integer format into the format string and pass the address of an integer variable. Always match specifiers: percent d for integers, percent f for floats, percent lf for doubles, and percent c for characters. When reading characters after numeric input, a leftover newline can be read as the character; adding a space before the character specifier in the format string consumes whitespace and avoids this issue. Common mistakes include forgetting the address-of operator, which causes the function to attempt writing to an invalid memory location and typically crashes the program, or using the wrong specifier, which leads to incorrect stored values. Practice reading an int, a float, and a char, checking that each value prints back as expected. Also consider checking the function's return value to confirm how many items were successfully read for more robust programs.

keyIdea.title: scanf essentials
keyIdea.text: scanf reads formatted input and needs variable addresses; match format specifiers and use a leading space before %c to consume leftover whitespace.

content.html:
Process Flow

scanf: format, address, store

1. Prepare a variable of the correct type and size.
2. Call scanf with a format string that uses the proper specifier.
3. Pass the address of the variable using the address-of operator so scanf can write into it.
4. Check the return value when you need robust validation.
Quick examples
int age;
printf("Enter age: ");
scanf("%d", &age);

float height;
printf("Enter height: ");
scanf("%f", &height);

char initial;
printf("Enter initial: ");
scanf(" %c", &initial); // leading space skips leftover newline
Common mistakes & tips
  • • Forgetting & causes scanf to treat the current variable value as an address, which usually crashes.
  • • Using %f for double or vice versa will misinterpret bytes and produce incorrect values.
  • • When reading characters after numbers, prefix %c with a space to skip whitespace.
Check your understanding
Write a short program that reads an int, a float, and a char and prints them back. Intentionally try leaving out & to observe the error and then fix it.

screens.title: Example: Reading Multiple Inputs Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a complete, small program that reads three values from the user and prints them back. The program includes declarations for an integer age, a float height, and a char initial. Each variable is declared before use and read with scanf using the correct format specifier and the address-of operator. Notice the format string for the character includes a space before percent c. That space tells the input function to skip any leftover whitespace, including the newline generated when the user pressed Enter after entering a number. Also observe how the printf function uses format specifiers to format the output, including a precision specifier for the float. A common beginner problem is forgetting the ampersand or using percent f for a double variable. Try compiling and running the program with correct usage, then deliberately remove the ampersand to see the type of crash it produces. Understanding this small, safe pattern is a foundation for larger interactive programs that accept multiple inputs from users. Example: Reading Multiple Inputs Safely means declare variables, use scanf with matching specifiers and &, and handle %c with a leading space to avoid leftover-newline reads.. In practical terms, a complete main program that reads age, height, and initial. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Example program
keyIdea.text: Declare variables, use scanf with matching specifiers and &, and handle %c with a leading space to avoid leftover-newline reads.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Read age, height, and initial

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  int user_age;
  float user_height;
  char user_initial;

  printf("Enter your age: ");
  scanf("%d", &user_age);

  printf("Enter your height in meters (e.g., 1.75): ");
  scanf("%f", &user_height);

  printf("Enter your first initial: ");
  scanf(" %c", &user_initial); // leading space skips newline

  printf("You are %d years old, %.2f meters tall, and your initial is %c.
",
         user_age, user_height, user_initial);

  return 0;
}
Annotations
  • • Each variable is declared before use so the compiler reserves memory.
  • • scanf format specifiers match the variable types exactly.
  • • The address-of operator provides locations for scanf to write into.
  • • The printf call formats the output and shows the stored values, verifying successful reads.
Pro tip
Always test with unexpected input, like letters where numbers are expected, to observe how scanf behaves. For production code, consider safer input parsing techniques.

screens.title: Address-of Operator (&) and Why It's Required
screens.narratorSegment: The address-of operator returns the memory location of a variable rather than its stored value. When you call the input function to read a value, the function needs a place in memory where it can store the incoming data. Passing a variable name without the address-of operator gives the function the current value stored in that variable, which is not a valid memory address in general. If the function tries to use that value as a pointer and write into it, the program will likely crash or exhibit undefined behavior. For example, when you write ampersand age in the call to scanf, you provide the exact memory address where the integer should be stored. This direct memory write is how input is placed into your variable. Beginners sometimes forget the ampersand, or pass an expression instead of an address; both cases lead to runtime errors. A concrete test is to write a short program that omits the ampersand and observe the failure, then add it back and see the successful behavior. Remember, scanf cannot guess where to store values — you must give it the address.

keyIdea.title: Why & matters
keyIdea.text: The address-of operator gives scanf a memory location to write into; omitting it causes writes to invalid addresses and often crashes.

content.html:
Definition

Address-of operator

Using ampersand before a variable returns its memory address, which is required for functions that write into memory locations.

Example contrast
// Correct
int age;
scanf("%d", &age);

// Incorrect — likely crash
int age2;
scanf("%d", age2); // age2 value treated as address
Common misconception

Beginners sometimes believe the input function can infer where to store a value from the variable name alone. In C, you must explicitly pass the address of the variable to enable direct memory writes.

Check your understanding
Write a short program that omits the ampersand, run it to see the error, then correct it to see the successful read. This concrete comparison helps cement why ampersand is required.
Key Takeaway

Always pass the address of a variable to scanf so it can safely write user input into memory.

screens.title: Arithmetic Operators and Precedence
screens.narratorSegment: C provides the familiar arithmetic operators: plus for addition, minus for subtraction, star for multiplication, slash for division, and the percent sign for modulus which returns the remainder of an integer division. Operator precedence follows standard mathematical rules: multiplication, division, and modulus have higher precedence than addition and subtraction. Parentheses can override precedence to make order explicit. A critical detail in C is integer division: when both operands are integers, the result is an integer with any fractional part truncated. For example, ten divided by three yields three when both values are integers. If you need a fractional result, cast one operand to a floating-point type so the division is performed in floating-point. Also be aware of the modulus operator's behavior with negative values — that can vary by implementation details and requires care. A common student error is assuming division always yields a decimal; confirm operand types and use explicit casting when needed. Try computing expressions with and without parentheses and with mixed types to observe how results change. Arithmetic Operators and Precedence means multiplication/division/modulus bind tighter than addition/subtraction; integer division truncates fractional parts unless you cast.. In practical terms, performing addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus with predictable order. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operator rules
keyIdea.text: Multiplication/division/modulus bind tighter than addition/subtraction; integer division truncates fractional parts unless you cast.

content.html:
Core Concept

Arithmetic operators

• + addition
• - subtraction
• * multiplication
• / division
• % modulus (remainder for integer division)
Examples
int a = 10, b = 3;
int q = a / b;     // q == 3 (integer division)
int r = a % b;     // r == 1 (remainder)
float f = (float)a / b; // f == 3.333... (floating-point division)
Operator precedence
Multiplication, division, and modulus are evaluated before addition and subtraction. Use parentheses to clearly express the intended order and avoid subtle bugs.
Quick checks
  • • Evaluate 2 + 3 * 4 → 14, not 20.
  • • Use parentheses: (2 + 3) * 4 → 20.
  • • Cast operands to float to avoid truncation during division.
Key Takeaway

Understand precedence and use casting to control whether division returns integers or fractions.

screens.title: Integer Division vs Floating-Point Division
screens.narratorSegment: Division in C behaves differently depending on whether the operands are integers or floating-point types. When both operands are integers, the operation performs integer division, which discards any fractional part by truncating toward zero. For example, when you divide fifteen by four with integer operands, the result is three, and the remainder operator returns three. If you want the fractional result three point seven five, at least one operand must be a floating-point value. You can force floating-point division by explicitly casting one operand to float or double, which promotes the other operand and yields a precise decimal result. Implicit conversions also occur: when a smaller type appears in an expression with a larger type, the smaller is promoted. A common mistake is assigning the result of integer division to a float and expecting the fraction; casting must happen before the division. For precision-sensitive work prefer double over float. Try both patterns side-by-side to see how casting before the division changes the stored result. Integer Division vs Floating-Point Division means if both operands are integers, division truncates. cast before dividing to get a floating-point result.. In practical terms, how operand types determine the result of a division expression. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Division in C behaves differently depending on whether the operands are integers or floating-point types. When both operands are integers, the operation performs integer division, which discards any fractional part by truncating toward zero. For example, when you divide fifteen by four with integer operands, the result is three, and the remainder operator returns three. Implicit conversions also occur: when a smaller type appears in an expression with a larger type, the smaller is promoted. A common mistake is assigning the result of integer division to a float and expecting the fraction; casting must happen before the division. For precision-sensitive work prefer double over float. Comparison

Integer vs Floating-Point Division

Integer: Both operands integer → fractional part truncated.
Floating-point: Any operand float/double → fractional division result.

float r2 = (float)a / b;    // r2 == 3.75  (cast forces floating-point division)

When computing averages or rates, cast before dividing so you retain decimals. For accurate accumulation or scientific calculations prefer double precision.

Cast before dividing when you need fractional results; otherwise integer division will truncate values.

Hands-on Activity

Area calculator walkthrough

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
  float length;
  float width;
  float area;

  printf("Enter the length of the rectangle: ");

}

Common Mistake

Diagnose & fix typical errors

• Missing ampersand → likely segmentation fault.
• Wrong format specifier → misinterpreted bytes and wrong stored value.
• Uninitialized variable → garbage values and unpredictable results.
Example fix
// Wrong
int n;
scanf("%d", n); // missing &

// Right
int n = 0;
scanf("%d", &n);
Debugging tips
  • • Read compiler warnings and treat them seriously.
  • • Add prints after each input to confirm values were stored as expected.
  • • Initialize variables at declaration to make behavior deterministic.
Quick fix

When in doubt, initialize, match specifiers, and pass addresses. These three changes fix most early bugs.

screens.title: Type Casting and Implicit Conversion
screens.narratorSegment: Type casting explicitly converts a value from one data type to another and is essential when you want to control how expressions are evaluated. In C you can write cast expressions that put a target type in parentheses before a value, for example casting an integer to float before dividing. This forces the division to be performed using floating-point arithmetic, producing a fractional result rather than an integer-truncated result. C also performs implicit promotions in mixed-type expressions: a smaller type is promoted to a larger one to prevent data loss. However, relying on implicit conversions can be confusing; explicit casting documents intent and avoids surprises. A concrete example is computing the average of two integers: cast one operand to float before dividing, store the result in a float or double, and then print with a decimal format. Avoid casting that masks real precision loss, and prefer converting to a wider type like double when accuracy is important. Practice by computing averages and noticing how results differ with and without casts. Process

Casting before evaluation

1. Identify the operation that needs higher precision.
2. Cast one operand to float or double using parentheses before the value.
3. Evaluate the expression; the presence of a floating-point operand makes the whole expression use floating-point arithmetic.

float precise = (float)a / b; // 3.333333

// Or cast b instead:
float precise2 = a / (float)b; // same effect

Use explicit casts to make code intentions clear. When accuracy is critical, cast to double rather than float to gain extra precision.

Cast before division to get fractional results; explicit casts document intent and prevent silent truncation.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how programs remember values, how to describe those values to the compiler, and how to get data from a person typing at the console. We'll treat a variable as a labeled box in memory: a name identifies the box, and the data type describes what kind of item fits inside. You'll see the core types every C programmer uses: whole numbers, single and double precision decimals, and single characters. Then we'll practice reading values with the standard input function and explain why the address-of operator is essential when storing user input. We'll also cover simple arithmetic, how integer division truncates results, and how casting lets you get precise floating-point answers. Together these skills let you build interactive programs such as calculators or small data collectors. By the end you will be able to declare and initialize variables, read and store user input correctly, and choose the right type and conversions to avoid common mistakes like segmentation faults or silent precision loss. Ready to build a memory model and work with real input? Let's explore the key topics that follow.

Over the next screens you will practice four fundamental skills. First, you will declare and initialize variables so your program has named places to store values. I will show why initialization prevents unpredictable behavior and how to pick descriptive names. Second, you will distinguish the core C data types — whole numbers, single and double precision decimals, and character storage — and learn typical uses for each. Third, you will use the standard input function to read values typed by a user and understand why the address-of operator is required for scanf to place values into memory. Fourth, you will perform arithmetic and learn how integer division differs from floating-point division, plus how explicit casting fixes precision issues. Each objective includes a short practice or checkpoint so you can verify your competency. These skills are the foundation for building interactive command-line tools and safe numeric calculations, so mastering them now saves time and frustrating bugs later.

This page breaks the objectives into concrete checks so you know when you've learned each skill. For declarations and initialization, create variables of different types and print their values. For data types, decide which type fits a scenario — for example, counts should use integers while measured values often use floating-point. For reading input, practice using scanf with the right format specifier and the address-of operator; also test reading a character after numbers and learn to include a leading space in the format string to avoid reading leftover newline characters. For arithmetic and casting, calculate sums, integer division results, and then cast to float to compute a precise average. After each task, reflect on common mistakes: uninitialized variables, mismatched format specifiers, forgetting the ampersand, and implicit truncation. These checks help you build reliable, interactive programs that behave predictably when users type data.

A variable is a label for a location in the computer's memory where a value can be stored and changed while the program runs. Think of it like a labeled box on a shelf: the label is the variable name and the box holds a value of a particular kind. Declaring a variable tells the compiler the label and the kind of box you want. Initializing a variable means you put a starting value inside the labeled box right away, which avoids unpredictable contents. For example, declaring an integer named count reserves space for a whole number and initializing it to zero gives it a known starting state. A common beginner mistake is using a variable before it has been initialized, which leaves whatever data was already in that memory cell and can lead to confusing outputs or logic errors. When naming variables, choose descriptive names and follow the convention used in this course; in C, snake_case is common and names cannot start with digits or include special characters beyond the underscore. By mastering declaration and initialization you create reliable programs that behave predictably when they read, compute, and print values.

C provides a small set of fundamental types that cover most beginner needs. The integer type stores whole numbers and is efficient for counts and indexes. Float is single-precision floating-point suitable for simple decimal values and when memory efficiency matters. Double is double-precision floating-point; it offers higher accuracy and is the default choice when precision matters. Character stores a single symbol and is often used for letters, digits, or to hold small integer codes. Each type uses a certain number of bytes which affects the range and precision. For example, integer division between two integers truncates any fractional part, so 10 divided by 3 becomes three. A common misuse is picking float when double is needed for accurate results, or assuming char stores multi-character strings. Another pitfall is forgetting the float literal suffix for some languages — in C, you often write 9.99f for a float literal, while doubles can be written without a suffix. Practice deciding a type for a scenario: counts use int, measurement with moderate precision can use float, scientific data should prefer double, and single typed symbols use char. This matching avoids precision loss and storage surprises.

Reading user input in C is commonly done with the standard input function that uses format specifiers to know what type to expect. The crucial detail is that scanf needs the memory address where the value should be stored. The address-of operator returns that memory address. For example, when reading an integer you place the integer format into the format string and pass the address of an integer variable. Always match specifiers: percent d for integers, percent f for floats, percent lf for doubles, and percent c for characters. When reading characters after numeric input, a leftover newline can be read as the character; adding a space before the character specifier in the format string consumes whitespace and avoids this issue. Common mistakes include forgetting the address-of operator, which causes the function to attempt writing to an invalid memory location and typically crashes the program, or using the wrong specifier, which leads to incorrect stored values. Practice reading an int, a float, and a char, checking that each value prints back as expected. Also consider checking the function's return value to confirm how many items were successfully read for more robust programs.

Also observe how the printf function uses format specifiers to format the output, including a precision specifier for the float. When you call the input function to read a value, the function needs a place in memory where it can store the incoming data.
